catalog_citation: Mathangwane, Joyce T. 1996. Ikalanga Phonetics and Phonology: A Synchronic and Diachronic Study. PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley (eScholarship qt8m17f977).
catalog_quote: [p.250] Ikalanga, as in many other Bantu languages, has an underlying two-tone system, that is a High and a Low tone. A number of words are found in which the only contrastive element between two words is tone. (18) below gives tonal pairs of words which illustrate this point. ... [p.255] As mentioned in §3.2, Ikalanga does not have distinctive vowel length; the vowel length we see in these examples is a result of the Penultimate Lengthening Rule, applying at the right edge of an intonational phrase (IP). (21) Penultimate Lengthening Rule (Hyman& Mathangwane (to appear) ... [p.41] target words were recorded embedded in carrier phrases ... to avoid the application of the phonological rule of Penultimate Length which lengthens the penultimate vowel in Ikalanga words when they occur in isolation or at the end of a intonational phrase.
sweep_summary: kala1384 Kalanga (Ikalanga): in catalog as 'tonal' on Mathangwane 1996 (UC Berkeley dissertation). this search of works with stress in the title had one item, Rodewald 1994 'Suprasegmental features and orthographic considerations in Ikalanga', an in-house paper in the Kalanga Bible Translation Project's 1994 research-conference proceedings (Francistown). Its bibliographic record was confirmed on Glottolog 5.3 and on the kalanga.org linguistics bibliography (which lists the proceedings' full contents, including Chebanne & Rodewald 'Kalanga tone and word division'), but no open copy, DOI, or library record was found; Crossref, archive.org and kalanga.org have no text, and OpenAlex/Google Books/Semantic Scholar/web search quotas were exhausted while HathiTrust, Google Scholar and SIL could not be reached by automated download/challenge pages. Relevance is unclear (title-level: suprasegmentals of this language, probably tone and penultimate length for orthography); priority medium. Nothing new was read; the catalog's deciding source was re-read held by the project (Mathangwane 1996 §7.3.1.1 p.255: 'Ikalanga does not have distinctive vowel length; the vowel length we see in these examples is a result of the Penultimate Lengthening Rule, applying at the right edge of an intonational phrase (IP).'; the dissertation text contains no occurrence of 'stress' or 'prominence'), and Hyman 2009 (already in the folder) confirms Ikalanga penultimate lengthening as a phrase-level, mora-adding process (p.196 ex. (4), p.199 table (7)); both support the 'tonal' coding and no source supersedes it. A side lead outside the list of works with stress in the title: Chebanne 2010 'Kalanga phonology, morpho-phonology..' (ZIJLC 1(1)) had an open PDF link on kalanga.org (ssrct.org), now dead; with and updated.

tone_statements.quote: A second language that has voiceless aspirates as depressors is Ikalanga, spoken in Botswana. Mathangwane (1999:196) distinguishes three types of voiceless aspirates in Ikalanga - regular aspirates /ph, th, kh/, labialised aspirates /pkwh, kwh/ (historically derived from velarisation), and a special set of "breathy aspirates" /pɦ, tɦ/. The first two types are regular voiceless aspirates that are non-depressors.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: all three deciding passages are verbatim in the Mathangwane 1996 PDF we hold/text at exactly the stated printed/pdf pages (250/268, 255/273, 41/59). The deciding source is a 400+-page Berkeley phonetics-and-phonology dissertation by a native-speaker linguist, later published by CSLI (1999) and listed by Glottolog as the language's phonology; nothing in Glottolog's grammar list (CASAS summary grammar 2010, Wentzel 1961, orthography manuals, MS grammars) is a better authority on prosody. The dissertation never describes word stress; prominence-like effects are H-tone spreading and IP-final penultimate lengthening, and Hyman 2009 (held; copied to the kala1384 check folder) independently characterises Ikalanga PL as phrase-level and utterance-type-conditioned, confirming classification tonal with domain=phrase. sources.quote: p.196: 'compare the following realizations of /ku-túm-a/ 'to send' in Ikalanga (Hyman & Mathangwane 1998:199): a. non-phrase final ku-túm-á [kùtúmá] b. phrase-final ku-túm-á → ku-tuum-a [kùtû:má] ... when the vowel becomes lengthened in (4b), the penult becomes a HL falling tone followed by H'. p.199 table (7): Ikalanga has PL in declaratives, yes-no Qs, WH Qs, imperatives, hortatives, vocatives, exclamatives and 1-syllable words, not in ideophones or paused lists (data: Joyce Mathangwane p.c. 2008).

sources.note: Section on Ikalanga: it is a language with voiceless aspirates as tone depressors; following Mathangwane (1999:196) three aspirate types are distinguished (plain /ph th kh/, labialised /pkwh kwh/, and 'breathy aspirates'), only the last being depressors; reports Mathangwane's acoustic finding that depressor aspirates have longer VOT and longer high-frequency noise; notes prenasalised stops are non-depressors and that Ikalanga also has fully voiced depressors; uses these facts for a cross-linguistic laryngeal feature analysis of depression (tone lowering / HTS blocking).

sources.note: First-hand autosegmental account of tone in Ikalanga infinitives (native-speaker data): sec. 3.1 states 'There are two tone levels in Ikalanga: a High tone (H) and a Low tone (L)', combining into falling (HL) and rising (LH) contours; low tones outnumber highs so only H and contours are marked; tonal patterns of infinitives of several morphological types are derived (HL melody, left-to-right H spreading to contiguous unaccented positions); closes with a mixed tone-plus-accent proposal ('dynamic tonic accents' that attract H tones). n_tones = 2 (H, L) stated explicitly.
